<reason>A wins by keeping the central comparison intact: blocking by-right supply does not stop transit-driven demand, it redirects that demand into bidding up existing low-rent homes corridor-wide and uncompensated. A credibly separates by-right from no protections, arguing objective pre-demolition payouts and upfront vouchers can coexist with automatic approval, while B's conditional alternative increasingly relies on freezing occupied parcels and scarce vacant lots. B lands real pressure on timing and the non-binding nature of compensation, but never fully answers how preservation plus rent controls opens transit access to movers and newcomers rather than only shielding incumbents.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Most decisive was A's use of B's admission in Rebuttal 2 that owners of cheap rentals would not sell under mandates — 'and that is the point' — reframed in A's closing as a deliberate residential freeze that manufactures the vacancy scarcity B cited against vouchers.</best_rebuttal>
